mcqs.question: Jump Game's greedy solution tracks a single running variable, furthest. What information does this deliberately discard compared to a full search?
options: The specific path or sequence of jumps that achieves the furthest reachable index
Whether the last index is reachable at all
The value stored at each array index
mcqs.explanation: The algorithm only cares about the boundary of what's reachable, not which specific sequence of jumps got there — that's a deliberate simplification, and the topic's later slides justify why discarding the path information is always safe here.

mcqs.question: A DP formulation of Jump Game II (dp[i] = 1 + min over reachable predecessors) is correct but typically O(n²). What does the greedy version's O(n) advantage come from?
options: The greedy version solves a subtly different, easier problem than the DP version
The greedy version skips checking some valid positions to save time

The DP version's O(n²) comes from redundant per-position scans; the greedy version collapses the same information into a single running frontier, discarding no information that actually affects the final answer
The greedy version only works on arrays smaller than a fixed size
mcqs.explanation: Both solve the identical problem and give identical answers — the DP version explicitly stores and scans every position's best predecessor, which is redundant work the greedy running-frontier approach avoids entirely, since the frontier alone captures everything the answer depends on.

mcqs.question: Why is 'always take the single longest jump available at the current position' a wrong simplification of the Jump Game algorithm?
options: It's actually equivalent to the correct algorithm and just a different way of describing it
It only fails when all jump values are equal

A position with a small jump value can still be strategically important if it's on the path to a position with a much larger jump value further along — 'longest jump right now' ignores that, while frontier-tracking considers every reachable position's jump value
It fails only on arrays with a single element
mcqs.explanation: The correct algorithm considers the best possible frontier across every position within current reach, not just whichever single jump looks longest from where you are right now — a smaller jump at a well-placed position can unlock more total reach than immediately taking the biggest available jump.

mcqs.question: Why is maximizing the reachable frontier at every step always a safe greedy choice in Jump Game?
options: A larger frontier is a strict superset of what a smaller frontier could achieve — nothing reachable under a smaller frontier becomes unreachable under a larger one, so a bigger frontier is never worse
Because the array is always sorted before the scan begins
Because there's only ever one valid path to the last index
It isn't always safe — it only works when all jump values are positive
mcqs.explanation: Reachability is monotone with respect to frontier size — anything achievable with a smaller frontier remains achievable with a larger one, plus more becomes possible. That domination is what makes 'always maximize the frontier' safe as a local greedy rule, without needing to track which specific path produced it.
